candidates.attacker_control: Fully unauthenticated remote input. The attacker POSTs JSON to the public /jwt_auth endpoint with provider=oauth2, an existing (non-root) appid, and a token string of the form "<garbage>:<garbage>:<forgeable JWS>"; the third segment is used verbatim as the id_token. Its payload (base64url JSON) is attacker-chosen and contains "sub", "email", "name", "picture". The attacker can also craft the claim types/values and choose oauth2/oAuth2second/oAuth2third aliases.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the id_token is ever validated elsewhere: SecurityUtils.isValidJWToken (HS256 MAC over app secret + user token secret) exists and is used for Para-issued JWTs, but it is never applied to this id_token; no JWKS/issuer/audience/nonce verification exists anywhere in this class. Checked that the IDP profile response, when it succeeds, would overwrite forged claims (profile.putAll at line 323) - however an invalid attacker-chosen access token makes that request fail or return non-200 while the claims remain, so the bypass does not require the IDP to answer. Checked that the other providers (Facebook/Google/LinkedIn/Twitter/Microsoft/Amazon/Slack) authenticate only via server-side calls to the provider with the access token and do not trust client-side token claims. Checked that NewTokenHandler rejects the root appid and requires app existence but performs no other authorization on the provider token. Considered that JWT-auth clients may legitimately send an id_token; even so, identity selection from unverified claims is not safe (and User.readUserForIdentifier's email-based account linking amplifies it).
candidates.impact: Authentication bypass/account takeover: an unauthenticated attacker can obtain a valid Para JWT for an existing user of any non-root app (if the victim's OAuth2 sub is known, or the victim's email when search is enabled), and can also create arbitrary users with attacker-chosen identity fields (identifier, email, name, picture) that are then trusted by account-linking logic. The issued token is accepted by RestAuthFilter/JWTAuthenticationProvider and grants the victim's API permissions. Depending on app configuration this exposes private data and write operations.
candidates.prerequisites: The server is reachable (default) and the targeted app exists and is active (any non-root app; no OAuth2 settings are strictly required because the IDP profile request fails/returns empty and the catch block returns the claims-derived profile). For direct takeover the attacker must know the victim's provider subject (“sub”, the stored identifier is "oa2:<sub>") or, alternatively, the victim's email plus a configured search backend so User.readUserForIdentifier() can find and re-link the account by email. No credentials, cookies, or signature keys are needed.
candidates.root_cause: GenericOAuth2Filter.fetchProfileFromIDP() decodes the payload of a caller-supplied id_token with Utils.base64dec()/Jackson and merges its claims into the user profile without verifying the JWS signature, issuer, audience, expiry or nonce (lines 303-308). GenericOAuth2Filter.getOrCreateUser() then treats those unverified claims as authoritative: the account id is read from the configured id parameter (default "sub") and the local user is selected/created via User.readUserForIdentifier() with identifier prefix "oa2:" (lines 173-222). Because JWTRestfulAuthFilter.newTokenHandler() passes the raw client-supplied "token" string straight into oauth2Auth.getOrCreateUser() (JWTRestfulAuthFilter lines 143-191, dispatch at 311-312), an unauthenticated caller controls the entire id_token. User.readUserForIdentifier() also falls back to linking an existing account by the (equally unverified) email claim (User.java 672-687), so no knowledge of a password or provider signature is needed.
candidates.title: Unsigned id_token claims trusted in generic OAuth2 login (POST /jwt_auth) allow account takeover
candidates.trace: 1) POST /jwt_auth -> JWTRestfulAuthFilter.doFilter (line 112, path matches "/jwt_auth") -> newTokenHandler (line 144) reads the JSON body and gets provider/appid/token from the caller (lines 152-154). 2) getOrCreateUser(app, provider, token) dispatches provider "oauth2" to oauth2Auth.getOrCreateUser(app, token) (lines 311-312). 3) GenericOAuth2Filter.getOrCreateUser splits the token on ":" and assigns tokens[2] to idToken (lines 158-170), then calls fetchProfileFromIDP(app, accessToken, idToken, alias) (line 173). 4) fetchProfileFromIDP sees a "." in idToken, base64-decodes the middle segment and merges its JSON claims into the profile map without any signature check (lines 305-308); the subsequent HTTP profile call uses a bogus access token and its failure/exception path still returns the claims-based profile (lines 317-340). 5) The profile's "sub" (accountIdParam default) is used to compute the identifier "oa2:<sub>" (lines 175, 193) and User.readUserForIdentifier() reads or creates that account (lines 195-221; User.java 656-704). 6) If the identifier/email matches an existing user, that user object is returned and, after checkIfActive(), JWTRestfulAuthFilter.succesHandler issues a real Para JWT for it (lines 163-169, 245-259).
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime/HTTP verification was performed; reachability relies on reading the filter/injection wiring (JwtConfigurer.addFilterBefore, Guice member injection of oauth2Auth). It was not verified whether the upstream project intends this id_token trust (i.e., whether this code is original or a regression), and whether GenericOAuth2Filter may be disabled by configuration in typical deployments. The account-link-by-email path additionally depends on a non-mock Search implementation; the sub-based takeover path does not.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347) leading to Authentication Bypass / Account Takeover (CWE-287)

coverage_summary: Coverage: get_source_scope reports 199 model-visible files (no binary/sensitive/symlink exclusions); get_relation_scope reports 193 indexed files, 163 Java files parsed with 0 parse errors, 6 source files missing from the index, and no control-flow/data-flow/semantic-resolution analyses. I read the SecurityConfig/filters (RestAuthFilter, JWTRestfulAuthFilter, JwtConfigurer, SecurityModule, SimpleAuth handlers, Csrf/Ajax/Ignored/Rest matchers), SecurityUtils, the OAuth/LDAP/SAML/password/passwordless filters, RestUtils and Api1 handlers (CRUD, batch, _me, _settings, _permissions, _export/_import, links, search), App/User permission and account-linking code, storage/queue/metrics plugins, HealthUtils, CORS/GZip/Field/Error filters, and portions of ParaClient, AWSDynamoDAO/Utils, and core utils. The 6 index-omitted files were not identified individually and were not claimed as reviewed. No code, tests, or scanners were executed.
limitations: No execution, runtime reachability proof, or exploit attempt was performed; all conclusions are source-level.
The P1 index is syntax/navigation only (no data flow, no semantic resolution); 8,453 of 12,068 calls are unresolved, so some cross-file flows may not be represented.
6 source files are absent from the relation index and were not individually audited.
No tests exist in this snapshot, so intended behavior could not be checked against test expectations.
Spring Security rule-ordering semantics and the framework wiring (Guice/Spring filter order, abstract processing filter behavior) were reasoned from source, not verified at runtime.
It could not be determined whether the id_token trust is original upstream behavior or a regression in this snapshot; the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: SecurityConfig.filterChain() declares requestMatchers("/**").permitAll() before the RestRequestMatcher authenticated() rule and parseProtectedResources() (SecurityConfig.java:99-103). If Spring Security evaluates accumulated rules first-match-wins, the later rules (and configured security.protected paths) would be dead.
rejected_leads.reason: Framework ordering semantics were not executed/confirmed, and Para's own RestAuthFilter (registered via JwtConfigurer) independently enforces API authentication for /v1/** requests, so exploitability is unclear and the line may be intentional upstream behavior. Unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: User.create() accepts a client-supplied "groups" value and only forces ADMINS for the configured admin identifier, while groups is @Locked for updates (User.java:318-326, 71); an app that permits user creation could let a caller create an "admins" user (isAdmin() grants unlimited access in RestAuthFilter.hasPermission).
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like long-standing upstream design (groups is intentionally settable at creation, admins are expected to control the users-create permission), and the snapshot contains no code that strips groups on create or update. Plausible but weaker/ambiguous; not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: SAMLAuthFilter defaults SECURITY_WANT_ASSERTIONS_SIGNED / WANT_MESSAGES_SIGNED to false (SAMLAuthFilter.java:332-334), so SAML responses may be accepted without signature validation unless the app configures it.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires SAML to be configured and is an explicit, documented configuration default rather than a missing check in this snapshot; upstream-style behavior. Unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: CORSFilter defaults to all origins with cors.support.credentials=true (ParaServer.java:278) and reflects the caller Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials (CORSFilter.java:237-266).
rejected_leads.reason: Reflects origin only when credentials are supported; Para's REST API primarily authenticates via Authorization headers, and this appears to be the stock third-party filter plus upstream configuration. Unconfirmed/defense-in-depth.

rejected_leads.lead: Server-side outbound requests driven by app settings / object payloads: webhook targetUrl (River.java:177-226), Graphite host/port (MetricsUtils.java:349-364), OAuth2 profile_url/avatar download (GenericOAuth2Filter.java:310, 442-461), SAML metadata URL (SAMLAuthFilter.java:122-127).
rejected_leads.reason: These are features whose targets are configured by an app administrator; the privilege boundary is weaker than the submitted issue, and no clear external-attacker control was found. Rejected as the single strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: LocalFileStore/AWSFileStore concatenate paths without rejecting ".." (LocalFileStore.java:65-118; AWSFileStore.java:63-124), and HealthUtils reads/writes the root-credentials config file through FileStore.load/store (HealthUtils.java:126-163).
rejected_leads.reason: FileStore.load/store is only called internally with a config-derived path in this snapshot (HealthUtils), not from request parameters, so no attacker-controlled traversal sink was identified.

summary: Reviewed the Para 1.50.8-SNAPSHOT tree (199 files; 163 Java files parsed by the P1 index, 6 files not indexed, no tests in the snapshot). I traced the authentication/authorization paths around SecurityConfig, the JWT/REST/OAuth/LDAP/SAML filters, RestUtils/Api1 CRUD and batch handlers, App/User permission and account-linking logic, storage/queue/metrics plugins. The single strongest issue is in the generic OAuth2 login path: the server extracts identity claims (sub/email/name/picture) from a client-supplied, unsigned "id_token" and uses them to look up or create the local user, and this path is reachable from the public POST /jwt_auth endpoint. This permits unauthenticated account creation and, given a victim's OAuth2 subject id or email, login as that user (account takeover), after which the server issues a valid Para JWT for the victim.
